title: AI in Education #10: Five Things I Learned from Kris Boulton About Alpha School, Paying Kids, and Where AI Actually Fits
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton talks with Kris Boulton, who spent 15 years building carefully sequenced maths teaching designed to eliminate student failure and now runs Unstoppable Learning, about a day spent inside Alpha School in New York. Alpha has no teachers at all, only "guides" barred from answering academic questions, because founder Joe Liemandt wants the cleanest possible data set showing whether the app itself, not a helpful adult, is responsible for a child's progress. Boulton pushes back on the easy dismissal that Alpha only works because its families are wealthy, arguing that rich kids are still just kids with the same dysregulation and struggle as any other, while acknowledging the harder open questions about motivation and cost remain unanswered. He also surfaces a detail unique to this episode in the series: Alpha pays students roughly one to two dollars a day for hitting targets, which Boulton argues functions as an effective motivator even though it discomforts adults who feel it undercuts the gratitude a heavily subsidised education is supposed to inspire. On where AI currently fits, Boulton is precise: it has essentially solved the practice phase of learning (generating constrained, well-formed task sets at scale) but has not cracked initial instruction and expansion, where he says every AI model he has tested - including one fed his entire curriculum - still gets the sequencing of examples and non-examples wrong. He lands closer to Adam Boxer's scepticism than Carl Hendrick's optimism about AI transforming education broadly, arguing that change, if it comes, will be slow and expensive rather than sudden.
points: Alpha School has no teachers, only "guides" who are barred from answering academic questions, because founder Joe Liemandt wants the cleanest possible data set to show whether the app or a helpful adult is responsible for a child's progress.

Boulton reframes the wealth objection to Alpha: "rich parents are rich parents, rich kids are just kids," pointing to a dysregulated five- or six-year-old he watched struggle at Alpha as evidence money doesn't erase normal childhood difficulty.

Alpha pays students roughly $1-2 a day for hitting targets (Alpha bucks for younger kids, a spendable debit card for older ones), which Boulton argues works as motivation even though it unsettles adults who sense it undercuts the gratitude a subsidised education is supposed to inspire.

Boulton's clearest verdict on AI: it has essentially solved the practice phase of learning (generating thousands of constrained, well-formed task sets in hours) but has not cracked initial instruction and expansion, where every model he has tested still gets the sequencing of examples and non-examples wrong.

Boulton sides closer to Adam Boxer's scepticism than Carl Hendrick's optimism, arguing that whether Alpha-style AI-led schooling scales to a UK comprehensive is unknowable now and that any real change will come slowly, over decades, given the tens of billions in capital and retraining it would require.
quotes: Kris quoted Joe Liemandt, the principal of Alpha School: they want the cleanest data set they possibly can get. If a child is not learning, they need to know that it is because the app is not good enough.
Kris argued that whilst rich parents are rich parents, rich kids are just kids, with everything that comes with being a child.
Kris's sharper read is that paying kids pokes at a buried sense of gratitude. Thousands of pounds are already being spent on a child's education, for their benefit

For the practice - the task sets that come after teaching - AI is there. It is perfect, in his words. Set the constraints, tell it every question must match the form of what was taught, and it will generate thousands of usable tasks in hours
The average teacher will take what is already made, deliver it, and move on. And - his line, not mine - the average teacher is not listening to this podcast or reading this newsletter.
Change, if it comes, will come bit by bit, over decades. And then one day everything is different, and you realise it took 30 years.
